title: Bike, bus or train to work?
question: Which way to get to work arrives on time most reliably?

background: Someone who starts work at 9:00 tried four ways of getting there over two working weeks in March: **cycling along the river path**, **cycling along the main road**, **Bus 14**, and **the train with a walk** at each end. Each day they noted how many minutes the trip took, whether they arrived by 9:00, and, on the bus and train, whether they got a seat. The example is fictional, made to show how a plain table of observations becomes a report.
The record is a long table, one observation per row, kept by a phone tracker, a calendar and a weekly tally of seats; nothing else was written down.
story.intent: The commuter wanted the way to work that gets them in by 9:00 most reliably, and wanted to see whether rain changes the answer.
questions: Which way arrives by 9:00 most often?
How long does each way take, and how much does that vary?
Does rain change which way is fastest or most reliable?
story.rule: No rule was fixed in advance: this report lays out the record so a choice can be made from it, and it records no decision.

alternatives.Bike via river path: Cycling the quieter river path; longer in distance, away from traffic.
alternatives.Bike via main road: Cycling the direct main road, with traffic.
alternatives.Bus 14: The number 14 bus from the nearest stop.
alternatives.Train and walk: A short walk to the station, the train, and a walk from the station to work.

cases.dry: Dry days: the ordinary commute, seven of the ten days.
cases.rain: Rainy days: three of the ten days, to see whether bad weather changes the answer.

story.covers: Trip minutes and arrival by 9:00 for every day of two working weeks, by way and by weather, and how many days a seat was free on the bus and the train.
story.notCovered: Cost, comfort, exercise, safety, winter weather and any week but these two. One Bus 14 trip was cancelled and taken by train instead, so that day has no bus result.

readings.compared: Four ways to work in two groups: two cycling routes and two kinds of public transport.
readings.results: Both bike routes arrived by 9:00 on all 10 days and took about 23 to 25 minutes on average. The train arrived on time on 8 of 10 days (32 minutes on average) and Bus 14 on only 2 of 9 (37 minutes). On the train a seat was free every day; on the bus on 4 of 10.
readings.groups: Cycling, pooled over both routes, was on time every day and about 10 minutes faster than public transport, which was on time on 10 of 19 days.
readings.cases: Rain slowed the river path most, from 23 to 30 minutes, while the main road went from 22 to 24; both bikes still arrived on time. In the rain the train was on time on only 1 of 3 days and the bus on none.
readings.observations: Eighty-four observations over ten days; two are invalid, the day Bus 14 was cancelled and the commuter took the train instead.
